I see this piece of advice spouted everywhere but often with little to no justification. Assuming I'm meeting all dietary needs and maintaining a healthy balance of carbs, poly and monounsaturated fats and proteins, does it really matter whether I go out of my way to eat the "recommended" amount of vegetables and fruits a day?

To my understanding, even multivitamins are largely redundant if you eat an appropriate amount of food each day. By corollary, if I get enough folate, potassium, vitamins etc from the foods I eat, what does it matter if I ate zero vegetables or plates full of them?

I'm of the opinion that some of the benefits that come from a diet including varied fruits and veggies aren't well quantified. We simply don't know exactly how a vitamin or mineral may be slightly different if ingested from one format to the next, or how bioavailability might be affected, etc.

It depends on the fruits and vegetables you're talking about. Not all veggis are created equal. Red beets have been shown to increase strength training and cardiovascular performance. They are also a great source of iron. Apples, on the other hand, are mostly only good for a fructose fix and a little bit of fiber. Broccoli and Chia are great for performance training, but grapes are mostly wasted calories.

Keep in mind that it's not just your macros that count, it's also the package they come in. If it was just the macros, you could eat nothing but refined sugar, oil, fat, and protein powder. It would be incredibly unhealthy and you'd feel like shit. Fruits and vegetables come with fiber, vitamins, minerals, antioxidants, blah blah blah, etc. I'm sure you've heard it all before, but it's easy to lose sight of. Your body needs these things, and your gut will function better with them. Healthy digestion is the starting point of a healthy body.
